12.2. Initializing Strings

As stated earlier, the optimal way to initialize strings is by assigning a string reference to a string literal. Because of transparent optimizations performed by the runtime, it is imperative to know when two strings are equal. The semantics of equality for strings exist at different levels. Strings can be compared by comparing string instances, object instances, and their values. The default comparison operations in both C# and Java compare the strings' values instead of the object references. This is a reasonable feature considering that strings are commonly used, and because of interning, it makes little sense to compare strings as string instances or object instances. Listing 12.4 illustrates some of these semantic differences.

Listing 12.4. Initializing and Comparing C# Strings

using System;

public class StringTest {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    char[] c = new char[] {'H','e','l','l','o'};
    string[] strings = new string[4];
    strings[0] = "Hello";
    strings[1] = "World";
    strings[2] = "Hello";
    strings[3] = new string(c);

    Console.WriteLine("-----[ Comparing strings using ==
                     operator of System.String ]-----");
    for (int i =0; i < strings.Length; ++i) {
      for (int j = i+1; j < strings.Length; ++j) {
        Console.WriteLine("{0} = {1} {2}",i,j,strings[i] ==
                                                  strings[j]);
      }
    }
    Console.WriteLine("-----[ Comparing strings using ==
                     operator of System.Object ]-----");
    for (int i =0; i < strings.Length; ++i) {
      for (int j = i+1; j < strings.Length; ++j) {
          Console.WriteLine("{0} = {1}
             {2}",i,j,(object)strings[i] ==
               (object)strings[j]);
      }
    }
    Console.WriteLine("-----[ Comparing String using the Equals
                     method ]-----");
    for (int i =0; i < strings.Length; ++i) {
      for (int j = i+1; j < strings.Length; ++j) {
        Console.WriteLine("{0} = {1}
            {2}",i,j,strings[i].Equals(strings[j]));
      }
    }
  }
}

The output of Listing 12.4 is as follows:


Using == operator of System.String]
0=1 False
0=2 True
0=3 True
1=2 False
1=3 False
2=3 True
Using == operator of System.Object ]
0=1 False
0=2 True
0=3 False
1=2 False
1=3 False
2=3 False
Using the String.Equals method
0=1 False
0=2 True
0=3 True
1=2 False
1=3 False
2=3 True

In C#, the == operator of the System.Object method compares the references of the objects and returns true if the two references point to the same object, and false otherwise. The == operator is overloaded in the System.String class to compare the value of the strings instead of the actual objects they refer to. Therefore, in Listing 12.4, strings[3] == strings[0] returns true because they have the same string value. However, when both strings[0] and strings[3] are cast to the object and then compared using the == operator, they return false. This is because strings[3] points to a different string object.

C# also has the Equals method, which is similar in behavior to the == operator. Notice in the output of Listing 12.4 that comparing strings using the Equals method and the overloaded == operator gives the same results.

Java programmers must be particularly careful when dealing with the == operator and C# strings.

Note that in Java the equals method functions the same way as the == operator of C#. The equals method is defined on java.lang.Object, and by default it compares the object references. However, the java.lang.String class overrides the equals method and compares the String values. Both Java and C# support String interning, so both the JVM and the CLR create only one object from a String that has the same value. This is an optimization feature so that different String references pointing to the same literal value are internally stored as pointing to the same String object. The process of interning is transparent in both C# and Java.

12.3. The + Operator and Strings

You can manipulate strings in C# using the StringBuilder class, which is equivalent to the java.lang.StringBuffer class of Java. StringBuilder is a sealed class and therefore cannot be subclassed. Similarly, the StringBuffer class is final and therefore cannot be subclassed. However, instances of the StringBuilder class are not guaranteed to be thread-safe. In Java, StringBuffer methods are synchronized wherever necessary. Listing 12.5 shows StringBuilder in action.

Listing 12.5. A Simple StringBuilder Usage (C#)

using System;
using System.Text;
public class StringTest {
  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    StringBuilder t = new
StringBuilder().Append("It's").Append("My").Append("Life");
    Console.WriteLine(t);
  }
}

The output of Listing 12.5 is


It'sMyLife

The Console.WriteLine() method takes the StringBuilder object as a parameter, and the runtime calls the ToString() method on the StringBuilder instance. The ToString() method of the StringBuilder returns the actual string stored by the builder.

Java developers often assert that Java optimizes string concatenation. In Java, using the + operator on strings is wasteful, especially if some strings that are to be added are dynamic in nature. Unless all the strings that are added are static, the + operator in Java creates a new string every time it is to be added to the old string, and therefore a long string made up by adding several dynamic strings ends up creating many temporary strings (which are eventually garbage-collected). The Java compiler, though, is smart enough to optimize the addition operator when all the strings that are being added are literals.

Listing 12.6 is a Java program that shows three ways to add strings. In the first approach, all the strings that are added are literals. Behind the scenes, the compiler translates approach 1 to approach 2, and hence the two approaches are the same. Approach 1 is more readable and hence is preferred if your string is made up of only literals. Approach 3 is where a StringBuffer would be useful, because in this case, for every + operator the runtime creates a new String instance by concatenating to the preceding string.

Listing 12.6. Adding Strings (Java)

public class StringTesting {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    //Approach 1
    String s1= "It's "+"my "+"life";
    //Approach 2
    String s2 = new StringBuffer() .append("It's ") .append("my
               ") .append("life");
    //Approach 3
    Strings s3= "It's ";
    String s4 = s3+"my "+" life";
  }
}

Listing 12.7 illustrates the same thing in C#.

Listing 12.7. C# Version of Listing 12.6

using System;
using System.Text;
public class StringTest {
  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    //Approach 1
    String s1 = "It's "+"My "+"Life";
    //Approach 2
    String s2 = new StringBuilder() .Append("It's")
                .Append("My") .Append("Life") .ToString();
    //Approach 3
    String s3 = "It's";
    String s4 = s3 + "My "+"Life";
  }
}

In general, method calls are considered expensive; hence, if something can be achieved with fewer method calls, that approach is faster. We will compare the three approaches (Listing 12.7) of concatenating strings by comparing how many method calls each approach translates into. To do so we need to look at the Intermediate Language (IL) generated by Listing 12.7, as shown in Listing 12.8.

Listing 12.8. IL of Listing 12.7

1 // Code size 66 (0x42)
2 .maxstack 2
3 .locals init ([0] string s1,
          [1] string s2,
          [2] string s3,
          [3] string s4)
4 IL_0000: ldstr "It's My Life "
5 IL_0005: stloc.0
6 IL_0006: newobj instance void
[mscorlib]System.Text.StringBuilder::.ctor()
7 IL_000b: ldstr "It's "
8 IL_0010: call instance class
[mscorlib]System.Text.StringBuilder
[mscorlib]System.Text.StringBuilder::Append(string)
9 IL_0015: ldstr "My "
10 IL_001a: callvirt instance class
[mscorlib]System.Text.StringBuilder
[mscorlib]System.Text.StringBuilder::Append(string)
11 IL_001f: ldstr "Life"
12 IL_0024: callvirt instance class
[mscorlib]System.Text.StringBuilder
[mscorlib]System.Text.StringBuilder::Append(string)
13 IL_0029: callvirt instance string
[mscorlib]System.Text.StringBuilder::ToString()
14 IL_002e: stloc.1
15 IL_002f: ldstr "It's "
16 IL_0034: stloc.2
17 IL_0035: ldloc.2
18 IL_0036: ldstr "My Life"
19 IL_003b: call string mscorlib]System.String::Concat(string,
                                                    string)
20 IL_0040: stloc.3
21 IL_0041: ret
22} // end of method StringTest::Main

Line 4 of Listing 12.8 shows the IL of approach 1 of Listing 12.7. Instruction IL_0000 of Listing 12.8 shows that the C# compiler automatically concatenates the literals for approach 1. There are no method calls involved, and the C# compiler merely pushes the concatenated string on to the Main method stack.

Approach 2 is shown from IL_0006 to IL_002e (line 6 to line 14). Notice that the StringBuilder approach involves five method calls (one constructor, three append methods, and one ToString() method). Compared with approach 1, approach 2 is inefficient for adding literals. Earlier we said that the Java compiler treats approach 1 and approach 2 as similar. The CLR, however, does not treat the two approaches as similar. In fact, the + operator of the String has no relation to the StringBuilder class.

Approach 3 is shown between IL_002f and IL_0040 (line 15 to line 20). Notice how the compiler concatenates the My and Life literals and uses the static function String.concat() to concatenate the It's literal to the new My Life literal. If the compiler had instead used a StringBuilder, it would have had to create a StringBuilder (constructor called) and then call the Append() method, making two method calls.

Clearly, you should use the + operator in C# whenever possible in concatenating literals, and you can also safely use it when adding dynamic strings to literals. In Java, however, the use of StringBuffer is the only way to optimize the addition of dynamic strings to literals. It uses extra method calls, but that is less expensive than creating new String instances, something that would occur if we used the + operator.

Now let's look at splitting (also called tokenizing) strings instead of concatenating them. Listing 12.9 gives a C# example of splitting strings. Listing 12.10 is the Java equivalent. Note that in Java, the access to the individual tokens is sequential. The C# API is flexible because it allows splitting the string using multiple delimiters.

Listing 12.9. Tokenizing Strings in C#

using System;
using System.Text;

public class StringTesting {
  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    string s = "I equivocally deny the claim, but I will agree
                to it under other circumstances";
    string[] tokens = s.Split(new char[] {' ',','} );
    foreach (string t in tokens) {
      Console.WriteLine(t);
    }
  }
}

The output of Listing 12.9 is as follows:


I
equivocally
deny
the
claim

but
I
will
agree
to
it
under
other
circumstances

Notice that the string is split into words, and where there is a “,” in the string, it is replaced by a blank character. Java's java.util.StringTokenizer tokenizes a string based on a single delimiter, as shown in Listing 12.10.

Listing 12.10. Java Version of Tokenizing Strings

import java.util.StringTokenizer;

public class StringTest {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
  String s = "I equivocally deny the claim, but I will agree to
              it under other circumstances";
  StringTokenizer st1 = new StringTokenizer(s, ",");
  while (st1.hasMoreTokens()) {
    StringTokenizer st2 = new StringTokenizer(st1.nextToken());
    while (st2.hasMoreTokens()) {
      System.out.println(st2.nextToken());
    }
  }
 }
}

12.4. Regular Expressions

Pattern matching using regular expressions is a powerful technique for advanced splitting and fetching of content from strings. C# provides classes in the System.Text namespace for doing pattern matching.

Note that this section assumes that you know the basics of pattern matching. If you are new to pattern matching, you should take a look at perl.com for introductory material. A detailed discussion of regular expression techniques is beyond the scope of this book. If you would like to explore regular expressions, we recommend the book Mastering Regular Expressions, by Jeffrey E.F. Friedl (O'Reilly, 2002).

As of JDK 1.3, Java did not have a built-in pattern matching API. However, JDK 1.4 has support for pattern matching. The C# pattern matching class does not interpret the pattern for every match; instead, it compiles a small program, which is then run to do the pattern match. This magic of compiling a small program in memory is achieved using the classes of the System.Reflection.Emit namespace. (Reflection is discussed in detail in Chapter 22.) Using the classes of the Reflection.Emit namespace, you can directly write IL for the functions of that class. It's a powerful technique used by the System.Text.RegularExpressions class to create a custom-matching engine.

The regular expression (System.Text.RegularExpressions.Regex) is compiled by the compiler to a stand-alone assembly using the information from System.Text.RegularExpressions.RegexCompilationInfo. Table 12.6 lists some of the key classes of the namespace.

Table 12.7 lists the static methods found in the Regex class. These methods are the most frequently used methods when you deal with pattern matching in C#.

Listing 12.11 shows the use of some of the Regex class's static methods.

Listing 12.11. Regex Methods in Action (C#)

using System;

using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

public class StringTesting {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    string s = "mammagammarammadramma";
    string pattern = "mm";

    //IsMatch
    Console.WriteLine(Regex.IsMatch(s, "kk"));

    //Get matches
    MatchCollection matches = Regex.Matches(s, pattern);
    foreach (Match m in matches) {
      Console.WriteLine(m);
    }
    //Replace
    Console.WriteLine(Regex.Replace(s, pattern, "kk"));
    //Split
    foreach (string part in Regex.Split(s,pattern)) {
      Console.Write(part+" ");
    }
  }
}
Table 12.6. Classes Related to Pattern Matching
Class Description
Regex Represents an immutable regular expression.
Capture Represents the results from a single subexpression capture. Capture represents one substring for a single successful capture.
Group Represents the results from a single capturing group. A capturing group can capture zero, one, or more strings in a single match because of quantifiers, so Group supplies a collection of Capture objects.
Match Represents the results from a single regular expression match.

Table 12.7. Static Methods in the Regex Class
Method Description
Escape Escapes a minimal set of metacharacters (\, *, +, ?, |, {, [, ( , ), ^, $, ., #, and white space) by replacing them with their escape codes.
IsMatch Indicates whether the regular expression finds a match in the input string.
Match Searches an input string for an occurrence of a regular expression and returns the precise result as a single Match object.
Matches Searches an input string for all occurrences of a regular expression and returns all the successful matches as if Match were called numerous times.
Replace Replaces all occurrences of a character pattern defined by a regular expression with a specified replacement character string.
Split Splits an input string into an array of substrings at the positions defined by a regular expression match.
Unescape Unescapes any escaped characters in the input string.

Here is the output of Listing 12.11 (numbered for convenience):


1. False
2. mm
3. mm
4. mm
5. mm
6. makkagakkarakkadrakka
7. ma aga ara adra a

Line 1 is obvious because the term kk does not exist in the target string s, so a False value is returned. Lines 2–5 are the ToString() representation of the Match object. There are four instances of the mm string in the string s, and hence four matches are printed. Line 6 shows that the pattern mm is replaced by the string kk in the string s. In line 7, the string s is split using the mm pattern.

Consider the string mnmkkmnmkkmnmkkmnmkk and the pattern @(mnm (kk)?)+. Listing 12.12 shows the use of the Groups and Capture classes.

Listing 12.12. Using Groups in Regex (C#)

using System;
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;

public class StringTesting {

  public static void Main(string[]args) {

    string text = " mnmkkmnm1mnmkkmnm2mnmkkmnm3";
    string pat = @"(mnm(kk)?)+";
    // use 'x' modifier to ignore comments
    Regex r = new Regex(pat);
    int[] gnums = r.GetGroupNumbers();
    Match m = r.Match(text);
    while (m.Success) {
      for (int i = 1; i < gnums.Length; i++) {
        Group g = m.Groups[gnums[i]];
        Console.WriteLine("Group"+gnums[i]+"=
                  ["+g.ToString()+"]");
        CaptureCollection cc = g.Captures;
        for (int j = 0; j < cc.Count; j++) {
          Capture c = cc[j];
          Console.WriteLine("Capture" + j +
                    "=["+c.ToString() + "] Index=" + c.Index
                        + " Length=" + c.Length);
        }
      }
      m = m.NextMatch();
    }
  }
}

The output of Listing 12.12 is as follows:


Group1=[mnm]
  Capture0=[mnmkk] Index=0 Length=5
  Capture1=[mnm] Index=5 Length=3
Group2=[kk]
  Capture0=[kk] Index=3 Length=2
Group1=[mnm]
  Capture0=[mnmkk] Index=9 Length=5
  Capture1=[mnm] Index=14 Length=3
Group2=[kk]
  Capture0=[kk] Index=12 Length=2
Group1=[mnm]
  Capture0=[mnmkk] Index=18 Length=5
  Capture1=[mnm] Index=23 Length=3
Group2=[kk]
  Capture0=[kk] Index=21 Length=2

The first capture group is marked by the first bracket, and then the expression will match an mnm if the Regex engine matches the expression to the one found in the text. Then the second capture group, marked by the second bracket, begins, but the definition of the first capture group is still ongoing. This tells us that the first group must match mnmkk and the second group would match only the kk. So if you decide to make the kk match an optional occurrence with the ? metacharacter, then mnm or mnmkk will be matched.

Next, you end the first group and specify the + metacharacter to ask the expression to match one or more occurrences. Now let's examine what happens during the matching process. First, create an instance of the expression by calling the Regex constructor, which is also where you specify your options. By turning on the x option, you make the expression ignore the comments and all white space:


Regex r = new Regex(pat);

Next, get the list of group numbers (gnums) defined in this regular expression:


int[] gnums = r.GetGroupNumbers();

Next, perform the first match. Then enter a loop, testing the success of the current match.


Match m = r.Match(text);
while (m.Success) (
)

The next step is to iterate through the list of groups starting at group 1. The reason you do not use group 0 in this sample is that group 0 is the fully captured match string, and what you usually (but not always) want to pick from a string is a subgroup. You might use group 0 if you wanted to collect the fully matched string as a single string.


for (int i = 1; i < gnums.Length; i++) {
    Group g = m.Groups[gnums[i]]

    Console.WriteLine("Group"+gnums[i]+"=["+g.ToString
}

Within each group, iterate through the CaptureCollection.


CaptureCollection cc = g.Captures;
for (int j = 0; j < cc.Count; j++) {
  Capture c = cc[j];
  Console.WriteLine("Capture" + j + "=["+c.ToString()
      + "] Index=" + c.Index + " Length=" + c.Length);
}

There is usually only one capture per match, per group, but in this case, for Group1, two captures show: Capture0 and Capture1. And if you had asked for only the ToString of Group1, you would have received mnm, although it also matched mnmkk. The value of the group ToString will be the value of the last Capture in its CaptureCollection. This is the expected behavior, and if you want the match to stop after mnm, you remove the + from the expression, telling the Regex engine to match on only the expression.

Regular expressions provide a powerful technique to do any kind of string manipulation. The key to exploiting C#'s Regex class is to understand the syntax of regular expression patterns. Once you understand how patterns are interpreted, using the Regex classes is trivial. A good resource on routine regular expressions is the book Perl Cookbook, by Tom Christiansen and Nathan Torkington (O'Reilly, 1998).

12.5. Summary

  • Strings in C# are immutable. The String class cannot be subclassed, and, just as in Java, the CLR optimizes String objects through the process of interning. This means that strings having the same value are represented by the same String instance object.

  • C#'s String.Equals() method is similar to Java's String.equals() method; they both equate the actual value of the string. The == operator in C# is overloaded and compares the string values instead of comparing object references as in Java. To compare the object references of the strings in C#, you use the == operator on the object class.

  • Unlike Java, adding C# string literals using the + operator does not result in the use of the StringBuilder class. In fact, using the + operator for concatenating C# strings (literal or dynamic) does not have the same object-creation overhead that Java has.

  • C# has built-in support for regular expressions. The classes in the System.Text.RegularExpression namespace can be used for pattern matching.

Chapter 13. Formatting Numbers, Strings, and Dates

Although computers don't care about data types being represented as 0's and 1's, humans do, and so formatting of the data is essential for meaningful display. Formatting allows you to take routine data types such as numbers, dates, times, and strings and represent them in a format that is suitable for the end user.

13.1. Formatting

Java programmers are familiar with the java.text and java.util packages, which have a bunch of classes that deal with formatting objects to strings. In Java, you implement formatting by specifying pattern strings. Pattern strings are string literals that have special characters that are interpreted by the runtime to format the data type. The special characters usually indicate the degree of precision, the type of formatting to be applied (based on the data type), and the positioning of the data in the formatted string. Depending on the data type being formatted (numbers, dates, or strings), formatting pattern strings differ. Pattern strings usually work in combination with locale information (java.util.Locale) and specifications of the symbols to use in displaying the rendered pattern. Java allows you to override the pattern string and the locale information at the time of formatting. Formatting in Java therefore relies on three cornerstone concepts: pattern strings, symbols, and locale information. All these can be specified in the method calls to any one of the subclasses of the java.text.Format class.

The cornerstone concepts in C# formatting are format specifiers (Java pattern strings) and format providers. Format specifiers are string literals of characters indicating how the formatting is to be done. Like Java pattern strings, format specifiers consist of characters that determine how the formatting is to take place. Unlike Java, which implements the locale and the symbol information in separate classes, C# combines the two in one format provider interface called IFormatProvider. Classes that implement this interface provide the necessary information about the symbols and the culture (“locale” in Javaspeak) to be used in rendering the data type using the format specifier. Like the JVM, the .NET runtime uses the default provider settings applicable to your culture when formatting data types, and hence you need not always specify the providers. You do have to specify the format specifier (pattern) in order to do any kind of formatting.

There are three format provider classes: NumberFormatInfo, Date TimeFormatInfo, and CultureInfo. You can also specify a custom provider by implementing the IFormatProvider interface.

Unlike Java, which has the java.text.Format class and its subclasses to actually do the formatting, C# formatting is built in using the ToString method on the data type itself. The .NET Framework standard data types—such as Int32, Int64, Single, Double, Enumeration, DateTime, and so on—have their ToString method overloaded to accept a format specifier or format provider.

13.2. Number Formatting

Table 13.1 lists the format specifiers for number formatting. You can format numeric types using the ToString() method on the data types. The standard format specifier string consists of a special character followed by a sequence of digits specifying precision.

13.2.1. Currency Formatting

Listing 13.1 shows currency formatting. The format specifier to be used is C or c.

Listing 13.1. Currency Formatting (C#)

using System;
using System.Globalization;
using System.IO;

public class NumericFormatting {

  static float NUMBER = 334.456F;

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    TextWriter tw = Console.Out;
    PlainCurrencyFormatting(tw);
    CurrencyFormattingWithCustomProvider(tw);
    GreatBritainCurrencyFormatting(tw);
  }

  private static void PlainCurrencyFormatting(TextWriter tw) {
    tw.WriteLine(NUMBER.ToString("C"));
    tw.WriteLine(NUMBER.ToString("C6"));
  }

  private static void CurrencyFormattingWithCustomProvider
                                         (TextWriter tw) {
    NumberFormatInfo provider = new NumberFormatInfo();
    provider.CurrencyDecimalDigits = 3;
    provider.CurrencySymbol= "$";
    provider.CurrencyDecimalSeparator= "*";
    tw.WriteLine(NUMBER.ToString("c", provider));
  }

  private static void GreatBritainCurrencyFormatting(TextWriter
    tw) {
    CultureInfo culture =
           CultureInfo.CreateSpecificCulture("en-GB");
    NumberFormatInfo provider = culture.NumberFormat;
    tw.WriteLine(NUMBER.ToString("c", provider));
  }
}
Table 13.1. Format Specifiers for Numerical Formatting in C#
Format Character Description
C,c Currency
E,e Scientific
F,f Fixed point
G,g General
N,n Number
R,r Roundtrip
X,x Hexadecimal

The output of the Listing 13.1 is as follows:


$334.46
$334.456000
$334*456
£334.46

When no provider is specified, the number is formatted as $334.46, which uses the CultureInfo en-US (that is the equivalent of Locale.US). The $ symbol is used for the currency, and by default there are two digits after the decimal point, so the last digit (6) was the result of rounding. The third number in the output is a currency from a custom NumberFormatInfo. Note that the currency symbol had to be specified as $; it is not assumed to be $ by default. Because the plain instantiation of NumberFormatInfo is culture invariant, it makes no assumption about the currency symbol.

The next example is that of printing the same currency using the British pound. Note how the appropriate culture is obtained and the default NumberFormatInfo for that culture is used.

13.2.2. Scientific Formatting

The E and e format specifiers can be used to format numbers in the scientific notation m.dddE+xxx. One digit always precedes the decimal point, and the number of decimal places is specified by the precision specifier, with six places used as the default. The format specifier controls whether E or e appears in the output. Listing 13.2 shows an example of scientific formatting.

Listing 13.2. Scientific Formatting (C#)

using System;
using System.Globalization;
using System.IO;
public class ScientificFormatting {

  static double NUMBER = 2345334.456547554D;

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    TextWriter tw = Console.Out;
    PlainFormatting(tw);
    FormattingWithCustomProvider(tw);
    CultureSpecificFormatting(tw);
  }

  private static void PlainFormatting(TextWriter tw) {
    tw.WriteLine(NUMBER.ToString("E"));
    tw.WriteLine(NUMBER.ToString("E2"));
    tw.WriteLine(NUMBER.ToString("E4"));
  }

  private static void FormattingWithCustomProvider(TextWriter
      tw) {
    NumberFormatInfo provider = new NumberFormatInfo();
    provider.NumberDecimalDigits = 2;
    tw.WriteLine(NUMBER.ToString("E", provider));
  }

  private static void CultureSpecificFormatting(TextWriter tw) {
      CultureInfo culture =
             CultureInfo.CreateSpecificCulture("fr-FR");
    NumberFormatInfo provider = culture.NumberFormat;
    tw.WriteLine(NUMBER.ToString("e", provider));
  }
}

The output of Listing 13.2 is as follows:


2.345334E+006
2.35E+006
2.3453E+006
2.345334E+006
2,345334e+006

In Listing 13.2, the first method, PlainFormatting, merely modifies the number of digits that are put after the decimal point using the format specifier. The second method, FormattingWithCustomProvider, tries to limit the number of decimal digits to 2, but the runtime does not do so because of the E/e format specifier. The last method shows how French scientists would denote a number in exponential form.

13.2.3. Number, Fixed-Point, and General Formatting

The number format specified by the N or n specifier formats a number into a string that has commas. By default, the number is formatted with two digits to the right of the decimal point. You can control this by specifying the number of digits after the format specifier; for example, N4 or n4 would mean four digits after the decimal point.

The fixed-point format is similar to the number format except that it does not put commas into the formatted string. The general format string converts the value to either the fixed-point or the scientific format, whichever is more compact. Listing 13.3 gives examples of the three formats.

Listing 13.3. Number, General, and Fixed-Point Formats (C#)

using System;
using System.Globalization;
using System.IO;
public class ScientificFormatting {

  static float NUMBER = 85.56546F;

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    TextWriter tw = Console.Out;

    //Using the {N,n} format specifiers
    tw.WriteLine("The number format");
    PlainFormatting (tw, "n2");
    FormattingWithCustomProvider(tw, "n");
    CultureSpecificFormatting(tw, "n");

    //Using the {G,g} format specifiers
    tw.WriteLine("The general format");
    PlainFormatting (tw, "g2");
    FormattingWithCustomProvider(tw, "g");
    CultureSpecificFormatting(tw, "g");

    //Using the fixed-point {F,f} format specifiers
    tw.WriteLine("The fixed-point format");
    PlainFormatting (tw, "f2");
    FormattingWithCustomProvider(tw, "f");
    CultureSpecificFormatting(tw, "f");

    //Using the % format specifiers
    tw.WriteLine("The % format");
    PlainFormatting (tw, "###.##%");
    FormattingWithCustomProvider(tw, "###.##%");
    CultureSpecificFormatting(tw, "###.##%");
  }

  private static void PlainFormatting(TextWriter tw, string
    pattern){
    tw.WriteLine(NUMBER.ToString(pattern));
  }

  private static void FormattingWithCustomProvider(TextWriter
    tw, string pattern) {
    NumberFormatInfo provider = new NumberFormatInfo();
    provider.PercentDecimalDigits = 2;
    provider.PercentSymbol = "&";
    tw.WriteLine(NUMBER.ToString(pattern, provider));
  }
  

  private static void CultureSpecificFormatting(TextWriter tw,
    string pattern) {
    CultureInfo culture =
           CultureInfo.CreateSpecificCulture("fr-FR");
    NumberFormatInfo provider = culture.NumberFormat;
    tw.WriteLine(NUMBER.ToString(pattern, provider));
  }
}

The output of Listing 13.3 is as follows:


The number format
85.57
85.57
85,57
The general format
86
85.56546
85,56546
The fixed-point format
85.57
85.57
85,57
The % format
8556.55%
8556.55&
8556,55%

Note that when you use the French culture, the symbol “.” is replaced with a “,”. Note also that using the % specifier, the % symbol is changed to & in the last example because of the following statement in the code:


provider.PercentSymbol = "&" ;

13.2.4. Percent Formatting

Unlike Java, C# has no special percent formatter. However, the % symbol is used to indicate the percentage. The number is multiplied by 100 before it is displayed as a percentage. In Listing 13.3 the last method call shows percent formatting. Note that we introduced a new character in the format specifier. The next section discusses these custom format specifiers.

13.2.5. Custom Specifiers

In addition to the standard format specifiers we have seen, you can specify custom format specifiers. Custom format specifiers are similar to the ones in Java. The special characters in Table 13.2 are used for specifying custom format strings and have similar meanings to the ones in Java.

In general, the zero character (0) is used as a digit or zero placeholder. If the numeric value has a digit in the position at which the 0 appears in the format string, the digit will appear in the result. If not, a zero appears in that position.

Throughout this chapter we have used the ToString() function to format numbers. However, format specifier strings can also be passed to the Console.WriteLine method to format the output at the time of printing.

Table 13.2. Format Specifiers for Custom Formatting in C#
Character Result
0 Displays leading zeros if the number has fewer digits than there are zeros in the format.
# Replaces # with digits only for significant digits.
,{comma) Separates number groups such as 1,000. When used after a number, divides by 1,000.
% Displays the % character.
. Displays the decimal point.
; Separates sections.

The format specifiers follow the same syntax as when you specify them in the ToString() method, with a slight modification. Listing 13.4 shows how to use the format specifiers in the Console.WriteLine method. The specifier string is {0:00} here; the 00 after the : is the actual specifier. The 0 before the : indicates that the specifier is to be applied to the first argument of the Console.WriteLine call.

Listing 13.4. Using the 0 Character Placeholder (C#)

using System;
public class ZeroFormatting {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    Console.WriteLine("{0:00}", 55);
    Console.WriteLine("{0:00000}", 556);
    Console.WriteLine("{0:00}", 66464);
  }
}

The output of Listing 13.4 is as follows:


55
00556
66464

The # character behaves similarly to the 0 character, except that the # character is omitted if there is no digit in that position. Listing 13.5 shows the use of the # character.

Listing 13.5. Using the # Character Placeholder

using System;

public class HashFormatting {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    Console.WriteLine("{0:####}", 55);
    Console.WriteLine("{0:#}", 556);
    Console.WriteLine("{0:##}", 66464);
  }
}

The output of Listing 13.5 is as follows:


55
556
66464

Note that 556 is now not preceded with leading zeros.

The “,” character is used as a group separator. If a comma appears in the middle of a display digit placeholder (0 or #) and to the left of the decimal point, then a group separator will be inserted into the string. Listing 13.6 shows how this works.

Listing 13.6. Using the "," Character Placeholder (C#)

using System;
public class CommaFormatting {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    Console.WriteLine("{0:,###}", 55678);
    Console.WriteLine("{0:#,##}", 55678);
    Console.WriteLine("{0:#,#,#}", 55678);
    Console.WriteLine("{0:#,#,#}", 55678857);
    Console.WriteLine("{0:000#,.000}", 55678857);
  }
}

The output of Listing 13.6 is as follows:


55678
55,678
55,678
55,678,857
55678.857

Note that putting one comma first divides the number by 1,000 and places the comma at the appropriate location. Every subsequent comma added divides the number further by 1,000, and the commas are again added to appropriate places. You can scale a number by placing the comma character directly before the decimal point. For each comma present in this location, the number is divided by 1,000 before it is formatted.

13.2.6. Section, Hexadecimal, and Escaping Specifiers

Listing 13.7 shows the section, hexadecimal, and escaping specifiers. The section specifier is used to specify different formatting strings for a number depending on whether it is positive, negative, or zero. Sections are demarcated by a semicolon. If there are three sections (x;y;z), then format x would apply if the number were positive, format y would apply if the number were negative, and format z would apply if the number were zero.

Listing 13.7. Three Kinds of Specifiers (C#)

using System;
using System.Globalization;
using System.IO;

public class ScientificFormatting {

  static float NUMBER = 85.56546F;

  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    //Hexadecimal formatting
    Console.WriteLine("{0:X}", 58);

    //Section formatting
    Console.WriteLine("{0:##;#.000;(##.00)}", 57575.356);
    Console.WriteLine("{0:##,00;00.##;(##.00)}",-57575.356);
    Console.WriteLine("{0:##,00;00.##;(##.00)}", 0);

    //Escaping characters
    Console.WriteLine("{0:###;bs;bs#}", 345);
  }
}

The escaping specifier is in fact not a specifier but a way to escape characters so that they don't get interpreted at the time of formatting.

The output of Listing 13.7 is as follows:


3A
57575
57575.36
(.00)
345#

Notice that when the number is 0, the section specifier chooses the rightmost format for formatting the number.

13.3. Date and Time Formatting

This section explores the date and time formatting capabilities of C#. In Java, the java.text.DateFormat class provides methods such as getTimeInstance(), getDateTimeInstance(), and getDateInstance(). These methods take optional locale information to create a DateFormat instance. You can gain some level of control over the formatting by specifying whether the format to be used is LONG, SHORT, or MEDIUM. However, the formatted string always follows a standard pattern. To change that pattern and to gain finer control of the formatted date, you use java.text.SimpleDateFormat, whose constructor takes a pattern string. The pattern string consists of date- and time-related symbols. For example, consider the following Java code:


SimpleDateFormat formatter = new SimpleDateFormat ("yyyy.MM.dd G 'at' hh:mm:ss a z");

This code would print a sample date and time as follows:


1996.07.10 AD at 15:08:56 PDT

Here, the letters y, M, d, G, h, m, s, and z have a special meaning. Repeating y four times would indicate printing the four-digit year. M denotes a month in the year, and m denotes a minute in an hour. So the character case is important.

To avoid confusion between the Java characters and their equivalent C# characters, we will leave the introduction to Java date and time formatting right here. Suffice it to note that in C# you have similar pattern characters. As a Java programmer you would be wise not to assume that the characters mean the same thing in C#.

Table 13.3 was taken from the .NET environment help file for the DateTimeFormatInfo class. It lists the patterns available for formatting dates and times and their associated DateTimeFormatInfo. Earlier in the chapter we mentioned the IFormatProvider interface. DateTimeFormatInfo implements this interface and has the necessary constants for getting standard patterns and symbols for formatting. The format characters are case-sensitive; for example, g and G represent slightly different patterns.

Listing 13.8 shows a formatting example for dates and times.

Listing 13.8. Using the DateTime Formats (C#)

using System;
using System.Globalization;
using System.IO;

public class DateFormatting {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    TextWriter tw = Console.Out;
    //Hardcoded patterns
    tw.WriteLine("Format d:" + DateTime.Now.ToString("d"));
    tw.WriteLine("Format D:" + DateTime.Now.ToString("D"));
    tw.WriteLine("Format f:" + DateTime.Now.ToString("f"));
    tw.WriteLine("Format F:" + DateTime.Now.ToString("F"));
    tw.WriteLine("Format g:" + DateTime.Now.ToString("g"));
    tw.WriteLine("Format G:" + DateTime.Now.ToString("G"));
    tw.WriteLine("Format m:" + DateTime.Now.ToString("m"));
    tw.WriteLine("Format s:" + DateTime.Now.ToString("s"));
    tw.WriteLine("Format t:" + DateTime.Now.ToString("t"));
    tw.WriteLine("Format T:" + DateTime.Now.ToString("T"));
    tw.WriteLine("Format u:" + DateTime.Now.ToString("u"));
    tw.WriteLine("Format U:" + DateTime.Now.ToString("U"));
    tw.WriteLine("Format y:" + DateTime.Now.ToString("y"));

    //Using DateTimeFormatInfo
    Console.WriteLine(";bsn;bsnUsing the info class:;bsn;bsn");
    DateTimeFormatInfo info = new DateTimeFormatInfo();
    tw.WriteLine("Month Day Pattern:" +
        DateTime.Now.ToString(info.MonthDayPattern));
    tw.WriteLine("Year Month Pattern:" +
        DateTime.Now.ToString(info.YearMonthPattern));
    tw.WriteLine("Universal Sortable Date Time Pattern:" +
        DateTime.Now.ToString(
        info.UniversalSortableDateTimePattern));
    tw.WriteLine("Long Date Pattern:" +
        DateTime.Now.ToString(info.LongDatePattern));
    tw.WriteLine("Short Date Pattern:" +
        DateTime.Now.ToString(info.ShortDatePattern));
  }
}
Table 13.3. Date Formatting Specifiers in C#
Format Character Associated Property/Description Sample Format Pattern (en-US)
D ShortDatePattern MM/dd/yyyy
D LongDatePattern dddd, dd MMMM yyyy
F Full date and time (long date and short time) dddd, dd MMMM yyyy HH:mm
F FullDatePattern (long date and long time) dddd, dd MMMM yyyy HH:mm:ss
G General (short date and short time) MM/dd/yyyy HH:mm
G General (short date and long time) MM/dd/yyyy HH:mm:ss
m, M MonthDayPattern MMMM dd
r, R RFC1123Pattern ddd, dd MMM yyyy HH':'mm':'ss 'GMT'
S SortableDateTimePattern (based on ISO 8601) using local time yyyy'-'MM'-'dd'T'HH':'mm':'ss
T ShortTimePattern HH:mm
T LongTimePattern HH:mm:ss
U UniversalSortableDateTimePattern using universal time yyyy'-'MM'-'dd HH':'mm':'ss'Z'
U Full date and time (long date and long time) using universal time dddd, dd MMMM yyyy HH:mm:ss
y, Y YearMonthPattern yyyy MMMM

The output of Listing 13.8 is as follows:


Format d: 2/12/2003
Format D: Wednesday, February 12, 2003
Format f: Wednesday, February 12, 2003 11:59 PM
Format F: Wednesday, February 12, 2003 11:59:52 PM
Format g: 2/12/2003 11:59 PM
Format G: 2/12/2003 11:59:52 PM
Format m: February 12
Format s: 2003-02-12T23:59:52
Format t: 11:59 PM
Format T: 11:59:52 PM
Format u: 2003-02-12 23:59:52Z
Format U: Thursday, February 13, 2003 7:59:52 AM
Format y: February, 2003

Using the info class:

Month Day Pattern: February 12
Year Month Pattern: 2003 February
Universal Sortable Date Time Pattern: 2003-02-12 23:59:52Z
Long Date Pattern: Wednesday, 12 February 2003
Short Date Pattern: 02/12/2003

Most of these patterns have equivalent property representations in the DateTimeFormatInfo class.

13.4. Formatting Custom Objects

Objects can implement their own custom formatting merely by overriding the ToString() method to take the format string and the format provider. Listing 13.9 shows a sample Hello object that implements a format string. The format string can be s (short greeting), f (full greeting), or v (verbose greeting). The format provider can be used to specify the culture to be used for printing the greeting. The default culture will be en-US. For the runtime to recognize formatting strings, the object must implement IFormattable.

Listing 13.9. Formatting Custom Objects (C#)

using System;

public class Hello : IFormattable {

  public string ToString(string format, IFormatProvider
    provider) {
    if (format.Equals("s")) {
      return "Hi";
    }else if (format.Equals("f")) {
      return "Hello, what's up?";
    }else if (format.Equals("v")) {
      return "Hello, how are you doing? How was your weekend?";
    } else {
      return "Hi";
    }
  }

  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    Hello hello = new Hello();
    Console.WriteLine("{0:s}", hello);
    Console.WriteLine("{0:f}", hello);
    Console.WriteLine("{0:v}", hello);
  }
}

The output of Listing 13.9 is as follows:


Hi
Hello, what's up?
Hello, how are you doing? How was your weekend?

So far we have looked at formatting numbers, dates, and strings in which a value is displayed in a manner specified by the format specifiers. Now let's look at parsing, a process in which a formatted string is taken as input and an unformatted value is obtained from it.

13.5. Parsing

Date parsing is an attempt to parse a string formatted as a date. Numbers can also be parsed. Listing 13.10 shows parsing of dates and numbers. Typically in Java, a good way to quickly check whether a string is a date or a number is to parse it and check for any exceptions thrown. The same technique works in C#.

Listing 13.10. Parsing of Numbers and Dates (C#)

using System;

public class Test {
  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    Console.WriteLine(Int32.Parse("556"));
    try {
      Console.WriteLine(Double.Parse("45764"));
    } catch (FormatException e) {
      Console.WriteLine(e.StackTrace);
    }
    try {
      Console.WriteLine(DateTime.Parse("12/3/2002"));
    } catch (FormatException e) {
      Console.WriteLine(e.StackTrace);
    }
  }
}

Listing 13.10 shows a popular pattern for quickly parsing data. Using this pattern, you put the onus of parsing a string on the runtime.

13.6. Summary

To format dates and numbers in C#, you specify a pattern string called a format specifier. The format specifier is a string literal of special characters that are interpreted by the runtime. For finer control of formatting, C# also supplies classes that implement the IFormatProvider interface. These classes provide other specific information, such as the culture and the symbols to be used for formatting. Java's formatting also uses a pattern string, locale information, and information about symbols to be used for formatting. Unlike Java, C# has no format-related classes; instead, formatting is done through overloaded ToString() methods on the data type itself, an approach that seems more intuitive. The format specifiers that are used in the ToString method can also be used in other common places, such as Console.WriteLine, to format printed strings.

Chapter 14. Using Collections

Programmers seldom want to reinvent the wheel by coding custom implementations of standard data structures such as linked lists, hash tables, binary trees, and so on. They would rather concentrate on the application logic that uses these data structures. Fortunately, the makers of Java and C# address this problem by integrating the formal implementations of popular data structures into the API. Java's java.util package has a cornucopia of classes that are extremely useful for writing complex applications. C#'s System.Collections namespace has a similar arsenal of classes that can make life easy for the programmer.

This chapter introduces the classes in C#'s System.Collections namespace. We briefly outline most of the classes, giving examples and comparing the classes to their Java counterparts. This chapter assumes that you are familiar with the concept of data structures and have dabbled in Java's java.util package.

14.1. The System.Collections Interfaces

Table 14.1 lists the interfaces of the System.Collections namespace and their Java equivalents. Note that the Java equivalent interfaces are in the java.util package.

In the System.Collections namespace, the IEnumerable, ICollection, IList, and IMap interfaces constitute the core collection-based interfaces. The other interfaces are utility interfaces for iterating over the collections, comparing objects, and obtaining hash codes.

Of the core collection interfaces, both IMap and IList inherit from ICollection, which in turn inherits from IEnumerable. This inheritance structure is different from that of the interfaces in the java.util package. Whereas the java.util.Map interface does not extend the java.util.Collection interface, the java.util.List interface extends the java.util.Collection interface. This means that in Java, a java.util.Map and a java.util.List can never be interchangeable, whereas in C# it is possible to intermix the two as long as they are both treated as an ICollection or an IEnumerable.

Table 14.1. Interfaces of the System.Collections Namespace
C# Interface Java Interface Description
ICollection Collection Denotes an abstract concept of a collection. Defines the size, enumerators, and synchronization rules for the collection classes.
IComparer Comparator Defines a method for comparing two objects.
IDictionary Map Defines a maplike data structure for storing key-value pairs where the map is indexed to the hash code of the key value.
IDictionaryEnumerator N/A An enumerator dedicated for enumerating through the key-value pairs of a maplike data structure.
IEnumerable Enumeration This is the root collection interface in .NET. A collection is, after all, a sequence of objects that can be enumerated over.
IHashCodeProvider N/A Provides a hash code for the object using a custom hash function.
IList List Defines a list-based data structure. Lists usually denote sequential access.

The IEnumerator interface provides all that is needed to iterate over a collection. It has one property (Current) and two methods (MoveNext and Reset), giving you unidirectional traversal across the collection. Java provides an Enumeration and an Iterator interface. The Iterator interface allows you to remove the object from the underlying collection. Unlike Java, C# provides several concrete classes that implement the IEnumerator interface and that are geared to enumerate over specific collections.

The .NET collections library does not have any equivalent for java.util.Set.

Having a rich set of interfaces allows you to write your custom collection classes to implement those interfaces. For the most part, you will be happy with the standard set of classes that ship with the System.Collections namespace. Let's explore those in the next section.

14.2. The System.Collections Classes

Table 14.2 lists the classes of the System.Collections namespace along with their Java equivalents. Some of the classes in Table 14.2 share a common set of behavior rules, discussed next.

14.2.1. Thread Safety

By default, the C# collection classes are not thread-safe and therefore are similar to the Java 2 collections. Therefore, the C# Hashtable (Table 14.2) is equivalent to Java's non-thread-safe java.util.HashMap and not to the thread-safe java.util.Hashtable. Most of the C# collection classes have a Synchronized method that provides a thread-safe wrapper of the class. Java instead provides a method called Collections.synchronized Collection() on the java.util.Collections object, and you use this method to get a thread-safe wrapper for the collection classes.

For example, to get a thread-safe ArrayList in C# you write the following:


ArrayList states = ArrayList.Synchronized (new ArrayList());

14.2.2. Type Safety

Java collections do not enforce type safety, and therefore objects obtained from the collection must be cast to the specific type. Nor does Java provide any infrastructure for writing type-safe collections.

C#, on the other hand, provides the classes CollectionBase and DictionaryBase, which are abstract implementations of type-safe collections. These classes have the requisite hooks that subclasses can implement to enforce type safety. You will see an example of this later in the chapter.

Table 14.2. Classes of the System.Collections Namespace
C# Class Java Class C# Description
ArrayList ArrayList A list-based data structure whose size is dynamically increased. Allows array-like indexed access.
BitArray BitSet An array of bit values that can be either 1 (true) or 0 (false).
CaseInsensitiveComparer N/A Compares two objects, ignoring case sensitivity of strings.
CaseInsensitiveHashCodeProvider N/A Provides a hash code for an object, ignoring the case of the strings.
CollectionBase N/A An abstract base class for storing strongly typed objects.
Comparer N/A Provides case-sensitive comparison of objects.
DictionaryBase N/A An abstract base class for storing strongly typed key-value pairs.
Hashtable HashMap Represents a collection of key-value pairs.
Queue LinkedList Implements a first in first out (FIFO) collection.
ReadOnlyCollectionBase N/A An abstract class for storing strongly typed read-only values.
SortedList TreeMap A collection indexed by the key of a key-value pair and sorted by the key.
Stack Stack Implements a last in first out (LIFO) collection.

14.2.3. Immutability

Immutable collections are useful when you don't want the collection to be modified. In the following code snippet, a class creates an ArrayList, populates it with U.S. states, and returns this list. This list is mutable because the caller of the GetStates() method can add, delete, or modify the list.


public ArrayList GetStates() {
  ArrayList states = new ArrayList();
  //Populate states from database;
  return states;
}

To enforce immutability of the collections, you must make them read-only. In Java, you use the Collections.unmodifiableCollection method of the java.util.Collections class to make the collection unmodifiable (in other words, the structure of the collection cannot be modified).

C# provides two levels of immutability. Some of the C# collection classes (ArrayList, Hashtable) implement two public properties (IsFixedSize and IsReadOnly) along with the corresponding methods FixedSize and ReadOnly, which mark the collection as fixed-size and read-only, respectively. In a FixedSize collection you can modify the individual elements of a collection, but you cannot add or delete from the collection (change its size). In a ReadOnly collection you cannot add, delete, or modify the elements of the collection. To make the GetStates() method return an immutable list you would have to do the following:


public ArrayList GetStates() {
  ArrayList states = new ArrayList();
  //Populate states from database;
  return ArrayList.ReadOnly(states);
}

14.2.4. Accessibility

The collection classes ArrayList and Hashtable provide indexers. (Indexers are discussed in detail in Chapter 17.) Indexers allow these collections to be accessed like arrays. Instead of using the Java-like Get() and Set() methods, you should use the indexer notation to get and set elements of the collection. The following snippet prints the elements of the ArrayList using the array-like indexed notation. Even a Hashtable with string-based keys can be accessed this way.


ArrayList list = new ArrayList();
  for (int j = 0; j < list.Count; ++j) {
  Console.WriteLine(list[j]);
}

object value = new object();
Hashtable hash = new Hashtable();
hash["key"] = value;

You can use C# collections to store primitives directly without converting them into their object representations. Therefore, the following snippet is perfectly legal in C#:


ArrayList list = new ArrayList();
list.add(1);
list.add(2);
list.add(3);

This is because of the automatic boxing and unboxing of value types, as described in Chapter 7.

Now let's explore the classes shown in Table 14.2 and examine them through examples.

14.3. Using the System.Collections Classes

Let's first look at the core collection classes. These are classes that actually are collections and store data.

14.3.1. ArrayList

An ArrayList is a popular list-based data structure used for storing a sequence of objects. An ArrayList is like a dynamic array that can grow and shrink. The C# ArrayList class is similar to the java.util.ArrayList class. Listing 14.1 shows the ArrayList class in action.

Listing 14.1. ArrayList (C#)

using System;
using System.Collections;
using System.IO;

public class ArrayListTest {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    TextWriter pr = Console.Out;
    ArrayList list = PopulateList();
    ShowProperties(pr,list);
    ModifyList(pr,list);
    SearchList(pr,list);
    MiscOperationsList(pr,list);
  }
  //Fill the list with sample data
  private static ArrayList PopulateList() {
    ArrayList ll= new ArrayList();
    for (int i =0; i < 20; ++i) {
      ll.Add(i);
    }
    return ll;
  }
  //Show list properties
  private static void ShowProperties(TextWriter pr, ArrayList
                                                    ll) {
    pr.WriteLine("Capacity "+ll.Capacity);
    pr.WriteLine(""+ll.Count);
    pr.WriteLine("IsFixedSize "+ll.IsFixedSize);
    pr.WriteLine("IsReadOnly "+ll.IsReadOnly);
    pr.WriteLine("IsSynchronized "+ll.IsSynchronized);
    pr.WriteLine("Synchronization root"+ll.SyncRoot);
  }
  //Modify the contents of the list by adding, setting, and
  //removing
  private static void ModifyList(TextWriter pr, ArrayList list){
    list.Add(13);
    ArrayList subList = new ArrayList();
    subList.Add(-100);
    list.AddRange(subList);
    pr.WriteLine("ToString() "+list.ToString());
    list.Insert(0,-1);
    list.Remove(18);
    list.RemoveAt(6);
    pr.WriteLine(list[4]);
    ShowContents(pr,list);
    list[2] = 89;

  }
  //Show all elements
  private static void ShowContents(TextWriter pr, ArrayList
      list) {
    for (int i = 0; i < list.Count; ++i) {
      pr.Write(list[i]);
    }
    pr.WriteLine();
  }
  //Call search and find related methods on the list
  private static void SearchList(TextWriter pr, ArrayList list){
    pr.WriteLine(list.BinarySearch(10));
    pr.WriteLine(list.Contains(12));
    pr.WriteLine(list.IndexOf(14));
  }
  //Conduct miscellaneous operations on the list
  private static void MiscOperationsList(TextWriter pr,
                                          ArrayList list) {
    ArrayList subList = list.GetRange(1,2);
    ShowContents(pr,subList);
    subList.InsertRange(subList.Count1,list);
    Array array = list.ToArray();
    list.Reverse();
    ShowContents(pr,list);
    list.Sort();
    ShowContents(pr,list);
    pr.WriteLine(list.BinarySearch(13));
  }
}

Note that the ToString() implementation of the C# ArrayList does not have a ToString() on the elements of the ArrayList. Also, methods such as Reverse(), Sort(), and BinarySearch() are part of the ArrayList class; this contrasts with Java, which has a utility class (java.util.Collections) that contains static methods that sort, reverse, and search collections.

The ArrayList class is not thread-safe. To return a thread-safe wrapper of the class, you use the ArrayList.Synchronized() method. Nor is the ArrayList class type-safe. All elements of the ArrayList are stored as instances of System.Object. As shown in Listing 14.1, you can use the indexer notation to access ArrayList elements. You can have fixed-size and read-only versions of an ArrayList.

14.3.2. BitArray

A BitArray class is ideal for storing a number of grouped Boolean values. For example, consider a Web page with an HTML form consisting of several checkboxes. The state of the these checkboxes could be stored in a BitArray. Listing 14.2 shows how to use the BitArray class.

Listing 14.2. BitArray (C#)

using System;
using System.Collections;

public class BitArrayTest {
  public static void Main(string[] args) {
    BitArray falsebits = new BitArray(3);
    BitArray truebits = new BitArray(3, true);

    BitArray copyfalsebits = (BitArray) falsebits.Clone();
    BitArray copytruebits = (BitArray) truebits.Clone();

    PrintState("Initial false bits ", falsebits);
    PrintState("Initial true bits ", truebits);
    PrintState("true bits OR-ed with false bits",
                            truebits.Or(falsebits));
    PrintState("true bits AND-ed with false bits
                             ",truebits.And(falsebits));
    PrintState("true bits XOR-ed with false bits
                             ",truebits.Xor(falsebits));
    PrintState("Not false bits ",copyfalsebits.Not());
    PrintState("Not true bits ",copytruebits.Not());
  }

  private static void PrintState(string banner, BitArray bits)
{
    Console.WriteLine ("=== "+banner+" ===");
    for (int i =0; i < bits.Count; ++i) {
      Console.WriteLine ("Bit ["+i+"] "+bits [i]);
    }
  }

}

The output of Listing 14.2 is as follows:

Bit[1] False

The BitArray class is similar to java.util.BitSet, which can be used to execute a logical AND, logical OR, and logical exclusive-OR (XOR) on a group of bit values.

The BitArray class is not thread-safe. There is no implementation for getting a thread-safe version of this class. The BitArray class is type-safe. It is populated at the time of construction, and there is no add or remove method on the BitArray. The BitArray constructors allow only certain types to be passed to them (BitArray, bool[], int[], int, byte[]). You can use the indexer notation to access the elements of a BitArray. A BitArray is of fixed size; you cannot add or delete elements from it. You can have read-only versions of BitArray.

14.3.3. Hashtable

A Hashtable is a popular data structure used for storing key-value pairs. The keys are stored in Hashtable based on their hash code. Duplicate keys cannot be stored in Hashtable, and keys cannot be null.Hashtables allow for fast retrieval of a value based on the key, and they are ideal for storing property values or any concept that can be broken down to a unique key-value pair. The order in which the entries are inserted in a Hashtable is not the same as the order in which they are stored. There is currently no C# equivalent of the java.util.LinkedHashMap, which maintains the order in which the entries are added to the HashMap. As mentioned earlier, a C# Hashtable is not thread-safe and should not be confused with java.util.Hashtable, which is thread-safe.

Listing 14.3 shows the use of Hashtable.

Listing 14.3. Hashtable (C#)

using System;
using System.Collections;

public class HashTest {

  public static void Main(string[] args) {

    Hashtable table = new Hashtable();
    for (int i=0; i < 10; ++i) table.Add(i, 10*i);
    PrintTable(table);
    Console.WriteLine("Value of table [2] "+table[2]);
    table[4] = 54;
    table.Remove(6);
    PrintTable(table);
    try {
      table.Add(1, 67);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        Console.WriteLine(e.Message);
    }
  }

  private static void PrintTable(Hashtable table) {
    ICollection keys = table.Keys;
    foreach (object o in keys) {
        Console.WriteLine("Key "+o+" Value "+table[o]);
    }
  }

}

The output of Listing 14.3 is as follows:

Key 8 Value 80
Key 7 Value 70
Key 6 Value 60
Key 5 Value 50
Key 4 Value 40
Key 3 Value 30

Key 0 Value 0
